title: What Do I Do with the Remainder?
goal: I can decide what a remainder means in a story: round up, drop it, or make it the answer.

card.desc: Practice day for remainders in word problems. With beans and cups, Bailey sees one division (50 ÷ 8 = 6 R 2) give three different answers: round up (7 boats so everyone fits), drop it (6 full barrels), or the remainder is the answer (2 left over). Seven new words, including context and capacity.

win: You let the context decide, and every answer made sense!

slides.title: What Do I Do with the Remainder?
slides.text: Yesterday you found remainders. Today you decide what a remainder means in a story. Sometimes you round up, sometimes you drop it, and sometimes the remainder is the answer.

notes.do: Set out: 50 dried beans, 8 cups (the boats), 3 sticky notes labeled Round up, Drop it and Remainder is the answer, whiteboard and marker, paper and pencil, her book.
notes.say: "Same division, three different answers. Today the story decides, and you are the one who reads the story."
notes.ask: "How did last night's Show What You Know go? What is the maximum remainder when you divide by 8?" (7.)

prompts: Tell what happened in the part you read since Monday.
The Vikings of Berk live by the sea. How does the sea matter in the story? Give one example.

notes.do: 6 minutes. She holds the book and finds pages.
notes.ask: "How does the sea matter in the story?"
notes.listen: A real detail from the book. The last prompt builds description skills: three specific details, not "it was cool".

slides.title: Yesterday's long division
slides.text: Solve on paper. Type the answer with R.

items.q: Use long division: 85 ÷ 6 = ____   (use R for the remainder)
items.no: Go one step at a time. At the end, whatever is left after the last subtraction is the remainder.
items.hint: Start: how many 6s fit in 8?

items.why: 36 × 2 = 72, and 72 + 1 = 73. It matches the dividend, so the answer is right.
items.no: Multiply 36 × 2 first. Then add the remainder 1.

notes.say: Praise each step out loud as she writes it.

slides.title: Words for today
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read it out loud. Then use it in your own sentence.

words.meaning: The words and facts around something that help explain what it means.
words.example: The context of the story tells you what to do with the remainder.

words.meaning: The most that something can hold.
words.example: Each longship has a capacity of 8 Vikings.

words.meaning: In a remainder story, to go up to the next whole number so that everyone or everything fits.
words.example: 50 Vikings, 8 to a boat: 6 R 2, so round up to 7 boats.

words.meaning: To throw away or not use something.
words.example: For full barrels only, discard the remainder.
6 boats are not adequate for 50 Vikings. They need 7.

words.meaning: Sensible and useful in real life.
words.example: "6 R 2 boats" is not a practical answer. You can't rent part of a boat.

words.meaning: A long trip, especially by sea.
words.example: The Vikings packed their longships for a voyage across the sea.

notes.do: She reads each card and makes her own sentence. Write Round up · Drop it · Remainder is the answer on the whiteboard.
notes.say: "Context is the most important word today. The context tells you what to do with the remainder."
notes.ask: "What is the capacity of your water bottle?" "Where would you go on a voyage?"
notes.listen: Capacity: the most it can hold. Practical: makes sense in real life.

slides.title: One division, three answers
slides.text: Every story below is 50 ÷ 8 = 6 R 2. Read the context. The answer changes!

steps.text: 50 Vikings sail. Each boat has a capacity of 8. How many boats so everyone can go? 6 boats leave 2 Vikings on the beach. Round up: 7 boats.
50 fish go into barrels of 8. How many barrels are full? The 2 extra fish do not fill a barrel. Drop it: 6 full barrels.
50 cookies are shared equally among 8 friends. How many cookies are left over? The remainder is the answer: 2 cookies.

slides.tip: Solve first. Then read the question again and ask: what does it want?

notes.do: Hands-on: 50 beans into the 8 cups, 8 per cup, until she runs out (6 full cups, 2 beans in her hand). Leave it on the table for all three stories. She sticks the matching sticky note on the table for each story.
notes.say: Praise each one she gets: "Yes! The Vikings can't stay on the beach."
notes.ask: For each: "Can those 2 be left behind? Do they make a full group? Or is the question asking about them?"
notes.listen: The same beans give 7, 6 or 2. She explains why with the context.

slides.title: Your turn: 38 ÷ 5 = 7 R 3
slides.text: All three use 38 ÷ 5 = 7 R 3. Read the context. Type the answer.

items.q: 38 Vikings row across the fjord. Each boat holds 5. How many boats do they need so everyone gets across?
items.why: 38 ÷ 5 = 7 R 3. 7 is not enough: 3 would be left out. Round up: 8 boats.
items.no: Divide first: 38 ÷ 5. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?
items.hint: Can the leftover ones be left behind? If not, you need one more.

items.q: Fishlegs packs 38 eggs into nests of 5. How many nests are full?
items.why: 38 ÷ 5 = 7 R 3. Only 7 are full; the 3 left over cannot make another one. Drop the remainder: 7 nests.
items.no: Divide first: 38 ÷ 5. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?
items.hint: Can the leftover make a full one? If not, do not count it.

items.q: Stoick shares 38 apples equally among 5 dragons. How many apples are left over?
items.why: 38 ÷ 5 = 7 R 3. The question asks what is left over, so the answer is the remainder: 3 apples.
items.no: Divide first: 38 ÷ 5. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?
items.hint: The question asks how many are LEFT. Which part of the answer is that?

notes.do: She types each one. Before she types, she says which sticky note fits.
notes.say: Praise the decision first, then the answer.

slides.title: Round up
slides.text: When everyone or everything must fit (boats, trips, tables, vans), the leftovers still need a place. Add 1 to the quotient.

steps.text: 130 Vikings sail on a voyage. Each longship has a capacity of 8. How many longships?
16 longships are not adequate: 2 Vikings would stay home. Round up: 17 longships.

slides.tip: Clue words: "so everyone", "all of them", "how many trips".

notes.do: She solves 130 ÷ 8 on paper before you reveal Step 2. Praise each long division step.
notes.ask: "Would 16 R 2 longships be a practical answer?" (No. You can't sail part of a ship.)
notes.listen: "Everyone must go, so I round up."

slides.title: Drop it
slides.text: When the question asks for full groups (full boxes, whole sets, how many you can buy), the leftovers cannot make another one. Discard the remainder.

steps.text: Hiccup has 100 arrows. A quiver holds 6. How many quivers can he fill?
4 arrows cannot fill a quiver. Drop it: 16 full quivers.

slides.tip: Clue words: "full", "complete", "how many can he buy / make".

notes.ask: "Why not 17?" (The 17th quiver would have only 4 arrows; it is not full.)
notes.listen: "Only full ones count, so I drop the 4."

slides.title: The remainder is the answer
slides.text: When the question asks how many are left over, the answer is the remainder itself.

steps.text: Gobber shares 75 nails equally among 4 workers. He keeps the nails that are left over. How many does he keep?
Each worker gets 18. Gobber keeps 3 nails. The remainder is the answer.

slides.tip: Clue words: "left over", "keeps the rest", "how many are left".

notes.ask: "What does the 18 tell you here?" (How many each worker gets. It is not what the question asks.)
notes.listen: She can say what BOTH numbers mean in the context.

slides.title: What does the context say?
slides.text: Read each story. Tap it, then tap the box. You do not need to solve it.

items.text: 45 Vikings sit at tables of 6. How many tables are needed?
items.why: Every Viking needs a seat, so round up.
items.hint: Can some Vikings stand all night?

items.text: 45 pickles go in jars of 6. How many jars are full?
items.why: Only full jars count, so drop the remainder.
items.hint: Does the question ask for full jars?

items.text: 45 stickers are shared equally among 6 kids. How many are left?
items.why: The question asks what is left, so the remainder is the answer.
items.hint: Does the question ask how many are left?

items.text: Toothless carries 4 fish per trip. How many trips to carry 29 fish?
items.why: All the fish must be carried, so one more trip: round up.
items.hint: Can some fish be left behind?

items.text: Fish cost 9 cents. Hiccup has 58 cents. How many fish can he buy?
items.why: He cannot buy part of a fish, so drop the remainder.
items.hint: Can he buy a fish with the cents left over?

items.why: He keeps what is left over: the remainder.
items.hint: What does Stoick keep?

slides.done: Everyone must fit: round up. Only full groups: drop it. What is left: the remainder.

notes.do: She reads each story out loud and points to the sticky note on the table before she taps.
notes.say: Praise each decision: "Yes, the Vikings all need a seat."

slides.title: Solve and decide
slides.text: Solve on paper. Decide what to do with the remainder. Type the answer.

items.no: Divide first: 93 ÷ 8. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?
items.hint: Can the leftover ones be left behind? If not, you need one more.

items.why: 87 ÷ 6 = 14 R 3. Only 14 are full; the 3 left over cannot make another one. Drop the remainder: 14 pages.
items.no: Divide first: 87 ÷ 6. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?

items.why: 66 ÷ 4 = 16 R 2. The question asks what is left over, so the answer is the remainder: 2 nails.
items.no: Divide first: 66 ÷ 4. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?

notes.do: She does the long division on paper, then says which sticky note, then types.
notes.say: Praise the long division steps AND the decision.

items.q:
200 Vikings sail. Each longship holds 9. How many longships are needed?
200 ÷ 9 = 22 R 2. Which answer makes sense?
items.why: 200 ÷ 9 = 22 R 2. Everyone must fit, so round up to 23.
no: You cannot have 22 R 2 longships. A story answer needs a whole number that makes sense.
2 is the remainder, not the answer to this question.
With only 22, the 2 left over would not fit.

items.q: Hiccup has 60 cents. A map costs 7 cents. How many maps can he buy? What do you do with the remainder?
choices: Round up: add 1 to the quotient
Drop the remainder: use only the quotient
items.why: Only full groups count, so the leftovers are dropped.
no: Read the question again: does it ask how many are left over?
Read the question again: does it ask about everything fitting, or only full groups?

notes.listen: 23 longships; drop it for the maps (8 maps, 4 cents left).

slides.title: Remainder story steps
slides.text: Tap the steps in the order you use them.
steps: Solve it with long division: quotient and remainder.
Read the question again: what does it ask for?
Decide: round up, drop it, or the remainder is the answer.
Write the answer with a label.
slides.why: Read, divide, solve, reread, decide, label.
slides.hint: You solve first, then read the question again to decide.

notes.do: She says all six steps from memory before tapping.

items.q: A longship can hold at most 30 Vikings. What is that number called?
items.why: The capacity is the most something can hold.
no: A voyage is a long trip.
Context is the facts around something.
A remainder is what is left over in a division.

items.q: "16 R 4 quivers" is not a ____ answer, because you count quivers in whole numbers. (Use a word from your word cards that means sensible in real life.)
items.why: Practical means sensible and useful in real life.
items.no: It starts with pr-.

items.q: Which word means to throw away or not use?
items.why: To discard is to throw away or not use.
no: Round up means go up to the next whole number.
Adequate means enough.
A voyage is a long trip.

notes.ask: "Use adequate in a sentence about food for a trip." "Use context in a sentence about reading."
notes.listen: She uses each word correctly in her own sentence.

sets.why: To discard is to throw away or not use.

sets.q: Which sentence uses voyage correctly?
choices: The Vikings set off on a long voyage across the sea.
sets.why: A voyage is a long trip, especially by sea.
no: Voyage is not something you do to a number.
That is a quotient, not a voyage.
A voyage is a trip, not food.

sets.q: 6 boats are not adequate for 50 Vikings. What does that mean?
sets.why: Adequate means enough. Not adequate means not enough.
no: Not adequate means not enough, not too many.
Capacity is how much one boat holds.
Not enough boats is not practical.

sets.q: 98 sheep cross the sea. A boat carries 8. How many trips does it take?
sets.why: 98 ÷ 8 = 12 R 2. 12 is not enough: 2 would be left out. Round up: 13 trips.
sets.no: Divide first: 98 ÷ 8. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?
sets.hint: Can the leftover ones be left behind? If not, you need one more.

sets.q: A fish costs 9 cents. Snotlout has 77 cents. How many fish can he buy?
sets.why: 77 ÷ 9 = 8 R 5. Only 8 are full; the 5 left over cannot make another one. Drop the remainder: 8 fish.
sets.no: Divide first: 77 ÷ 9. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?
sets.hint: Can the leftover make a full one? If not, do not count it.

sets.q: 89 shells are shared equally among 7 friends. How many shells are left over?
sets.why: 89 ÷ 7 = 12 R 5. The question asks what is left over, so the answer is the remainder: 5 shells.
sets.no: Divide first: 89 ÷ 7. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?
sets.hint: The question asks how many are LEFT. Which part of the answer is that?

sets.q: 461 apples are shared equally among 6 barrels. How many apples are left over?
sets.why: 461 ÷ 6 = 76 R 5. The question asks what is left over, so the answer is the remainder: 5 apples.
sets.no: Divide first: 461 ÷ 6. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?
sets.hint: The question asks how many are LEFT. Which part of the answer is that?

sets.q: 52 Vikings sit at tables of 6. How many tables are needed so everyone sits? What do you do with the remainder?
choices: Drop the remainder: use only the quotient
Round up: add 1 to the quotient
sets.why: Everyone or everything must fit, so the leftovers need one more group. Round up.
no: Read the question again: does it ask for full groups only?
Read the question again: does it ask how many are left over?

sets.q:
A box holds 8 candles. How many boxes can be filled with 132 candles?
132 ÷ 8 = 16 R 4. Which answer makes sense?
sets.why: 132 ÷ 8 = 16 R 4. Only full groups count: 16.
no: There is no 17th full group: only 4 are left, not 8.
4 is the remainder, not the answer to this question.
You cannot have 16 R 4 boxes. A story answer needs a whole number that makes sense.

sets.q: Use long division: 526 ÷ 3 = ____   (use R for the remainder)
sets.no: Go one step at a time. At the end, whatever is left after the last subtraction is the remainder.

sets.q: In a remainder story, to go up to the next whole number so everyone fits is to ____ ____. (Type the two words.)
sets.why: To round up means to go up to the next whole number.
sets.no: It starts with r and u.

sets.q: Which word means the words and facts around something that help explain it?
sets.why: The context helps explain what something means.
no: Capacity is the most something can hold.
Adequate means enough.
A voyage is a long trip.

sets.q: For full boxes only, you should…
choices: add the remainder to the quotient
sets.why: Only full boxes count, so discard (drop) the remainder.
no: Rounding up is for when everything must fit.
Adding it changes the answer.
The remainder is the answer only when the question asks what is left.

practice.intro: Three tries on each one, but only your first try counts. Solve on paper first. Then let the context tell you what to do with the remainder.

questions.q: Toothless carries 3 fish per trip. How many trips to carry 58 fish?
questions.why: 58 ÷ 3 = 19 R 1. 19 is not enough: 1 would be left out. Round up: 20 trips.
questions.no: Divide first: 58 ÷ 3. Then read the question again: what does it ask for?
questions.hint: Can the leftover ones be left behind? If not, you need one more.

questions.hint: Can the leftover make a full one? If not, do not count it.

choices: Drop the remainder: use only the quotient
Round up: add 1 to the quotient
questions.why: The question asks how many are left over, so the remainder is the answer.
no: Read the question again: does it ask for full groups only?
Read the question again: does it ask about everything fitting, or only full groups?

questions.q:
110 Vikings sail. Each ship holds 8. How many ships are needed?
110 ÷ 8 = 13 R 6. Which answer makes sense?
questions.why: 110 ÷ 8 = 13 R 6. Everyone must fit, so round up to 14.
no: 6 is the remainder, not the answer to this question.
With only 13, the 6 left over would not fit.
You cannot have 13 R 6 ships. A story answer needs a whole number that makes sense.

questions.q: Enough for what is needed is ____. (Use a word from your word cards.)
A long trip, especially by sea, is a ____. (Use a word from your word cards.)
questions.why: A voyage is a long trip, especially by sea.

choices: You count quivers in whole numbers, so R 4 makes no sense.
questions.why: Practical means sensible in real life. A real answer needs whole quivers.
no: The math can be right and still not practical.
The size is not the problem; the R 4 is.
Quivers do hold arrows.

packet.title: What Do I Do with the Remainder?

pages.title: Part 1: Word Power
pages.directions: Draw a line from each word to its meaning.

items.text: 1. Match each word to its meaning.
right: to throw away or not use
go up to the next whole number
the facts around something that explain it

pages.title: Part 2: One division, three answers
pages.directions: All three stories are 46 ÷ 7 = 6 R 4. Write the answer with a label.

items.text: 2. 46 Vikings ride in boats that hold 7. How many boats are needed? __________
3. 46 fish go in barrels of 7. How many barrels are full? __________
4. 46 apples are shared equally by 7 dragons. How many are left over? __________

pages.title: Part 3: What does the context say?
pages.directions: Circle what to do with the remainder. Do not solve.

items.text: 5. Each tent sleeps 4 Vikings. How many tents for 35 Vikings?
6. Ropes are cut into 9-foot pieces. How many whole pieces from 80 feet?

pages.title: Part 4: Solve and decide
pages.directions: Solve with long division. Decide what to do with the remainder. Write the answer with a label.

items.text: 7. 150 Vikings sail on a voyage. Each longship holds 8. How many longships are needed?
8. Fishlegs has 213 cards. 6 cards fill a page. How many pages can he fill?
9. Stoick shares 95 coins equally among 4 warriors and keeps the rest. How many coins does Stoick keep?
10. Write your own dragon story where you must round up. Solve it.
11. Book corner: Describe a sea voyage or trip in How to Train Your Dragon, or one you would like to take.

teacher.objective: Bailey interprets remainders in word problems: she solves with long division, rereads the question, and decides whether to round up (everyone or everything must fit), drop the remainder (only full groups count), or give the remainder as the answer (what is left over), then writes a practical answer with a label.
materials: Class lesson on your laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)
3 sticky notes: Round up, Drop it, Remainder is the answer
Paper and a pencil for Bailey
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon
Packet (2 pages): page 1 on Wednesday, page 2 over the break

plan.do: Class slide 1. Beans, cups, sticky notes. Ask about last night's check; maximum remainder for ÷ 8.
Class slide 2. What happened since Monday, how the sea matters, a scene described with three details.
Class slide 3. 85 ÷ 6 and the check for 73 ÷ 2.
Class slide 4. Her own sentence for each word; the three choices on the whiteboard.
Class slides 5–6. 50 beans in cups of 8: 7 boats, 6 full barrels, 2 cookies. Then 38 ÷ 5 three ways.
Class slides 7–9. 130 ÷ 8 → 17 longships; 100 ÷ 6 → 16 full quivers; 75 ÷ 4 → Gobber keeps 3. She solves each on paper first; praise each step.
Class slide 10. She points to the sticky note, then taps the box.
Class slides 11–12. Solve and decide (93 ÷ 8, 87 ÷ 6, 66 ÷ 4); which answer makes sense.
Class slide 13. She orders the six steps from memory.
Class slide 14. Capacity, practical, discard; adequate and context in her own sentences.
Class slide 15. Three stories on her own; note which kind she misses.
Class slide 16. Course page: Tuesday night and Wednesday tasks.

watch: Writing "6 R 2 boats" as the answer. Ask: "Can you rent part of a boat? What is practical?"
Rounding up every time (or never). Ask: "Read the question again. Does everyone need to fit, or only full ones?"
Giving the quotient when the question asks what is left over. Ask: "What does Gobber keep?"
Deciding before solving and then forgetting the remainder. Keep the order: solve, reread, decide.
Long division slips in the 3-digit stories (130 ÷ 8: 8 does not fit in 1, start with 13). Praise each correct step.
"I can't do it" on a long story. Have her read it aloud and ask only: "What is the total, and what is the size of each group?"

packet_key.answer: context → the facts around something that explain it; capacity → the most something can hold; round up → go up to the next whole number; discard → to throw away or not use; adequate → enough for what is needed; practical → sensible in real life; voyage → a long trip by sea
95 ÷ 4 = 23 R 3 → the remainder: Stoick keeps 3 coins
Answers vary; a story where everything must fit, solved with the quotient plus 1.
Answers vary; uses voyage correctly with details.
